questions.stem: Orbitally induced changes in solar radiation are caused by variations in which three features of Earth's orbit and rotation?
options: Obliquity, sunspot number and the length of a year
Precession, rotation speed and the solar wind strength
Eccentricity, obliquity (axial tilt) and precession
Eccentricity, rotation speed and the Moon's distance
questions.explanation: These Milankovitch cycles change how solar radiation is distributed by latitude and season. Sunspots are changes in the Sun itself, not in Earth's orbit.

questions.stem: Which orbital cycle has a period of about 41 000 years?
options: Rotation, the change in the length of Earth's day
Obliquity, the change in the tilt of Earth's axis
Eccentricity, the change in the shape of the orbit
Precession, the wobble in the direction of the axis
questions.explanation: Earth's axial tilt varies between about 22° and 24.5° over roughly 41 000 years. Eccentricity varies over about 100 000 years and precession over about 23 000 years.

questions.stem: Ice cores show that glacial and interglacial periods over the last 800 000 years recurred roughly every 100 000 years. Which orbital cycle matches this period?
options: Precession
Daily rotation
Eccentricity
Obliquity
questions.explanation: Eccentricity, the change in the shape of Earth's orbit from near-circular to more elliptical, has a dominant period of about 100 000 years, matching the recent glacial cycles.

questions.stem: How does an increase in Earth's axial tilt affect climate at high latitudes?
options: Seasons disappear entirely, because both hemispheres receive equal sunlight
Summers become warmer and winters colder, so less snow survives each summer
Summers become cooler and winters warmer, so more snow survives each summer
Both summers and winters become colder, so ice sheets grow in every season
questions.explanation: Greater tilt sharpens the contrast between seasons. Warmer high-latitude summers melt more of the previous winter's snow, which works against ice sheet growth.

questions.stem: Orbital changes alter the total sunlight Earth receives only slightly, yet they trigger large glacial cycles. What best explains this?
options: Orbital changes trigger large volcanic eruptions, and these eruptions control the ice ages directly
The small changes act alone, because Earth's climate is not sensitive to feedback
Feedbacks such as changing ice cover and carbon dioxide release or uptake amplify the change
The orbit changes the Sun's own output, multiplying the energy it emits by many times over
questions.explanation: A small orbital push starts ice to grow or melt. Changes in albedo, and in carbon dioxide released or absorbed by the oceans, then amplify the initial change into a full glacial or interglacial.

questions.stem: How can changes in oceanic circulation cause climate change?
options: They change the length of Earth's year, altering the timing of the seasons
They change the composition of Earth's core, altering the heat released by volcanoes
They change how heat is carried around the globe, warming some regions and cooling others
They change the amount of energy the Sun emits, warming every part of the whole planet at once
questions.explanation: Ocean currents move vast amounts of heat from the tropics towards the poles. If circulation slows or changes route, regional and even global climate can change.

questions.stem: About 34 million years ago, ocean gateways opened between Antarctica and the other southern continents, allowing a current to flow right around Antarctica. How did this contribute to Antarctic glaciation?
options: The current removed all the salt from the Southern Ocean, so it froze solid
The circumpolar current isolated Antarctica from warm water carried from lower latitudes
The current carried warm tropical water directly to the Antarctic coast throughout the year
The gateways let Antarctica drift rapidly to the equator, where ice could form
questions.explanation: Once a current circled Antarctica, warm currents from lower latitudes no longer reached its coasts, helping the continent cool. Falling atmospheric carbon dioxide is also thought to have contributed.

questions.stem: The plate tectonic supercycle is:
options: the daily rise and fall of the continental crust caused by the gravitational pull of the Moon
the yearly movement of plates towards and away from the equator with the seasons
the 11-year cycle of volcanic eruptions linked to changes in the Sun's activity
the repeated assembly and break-up of supercontinents over hundreds of millions of years
questions.explanation: Continents periodically gather into a supercontinent, such as Pangaea, and later rift apart. This changes sea level, ocean circulation, volcanic outgassing and where land lies relative to the poles.

questions.stem: Why is the interior of a supercontinent such as Pangaea expected to have a very dry climate?
options: A supercontinent lies entirely at the poles, where no precipitation ever falls
Supercontinents have no mountains, so air cannot rise and form clouds anywhere
Joined continents block sunlight, so no water evaporates from the oceans nearby
Much of the land lies far from the ocean, the main source of moisture for rain
questions.explanation: Moist air from the ocean loses its water as it moves inland, so the heart of a huge landmass receives little rain. Large deserts and evaporite deposits are found in Pangaean-age rocks.

questions.stem: Uplift of a large mountain range exposes vast amounts of fresh rock to chemical weathering, which consumes carbon dioxide. Over millions of years this would tend to:
options: lower atmospheric carbon dioxide and cool the global climate
raise atmospheric carbon dioxide and warm the global climate
leave carbon dioxide unchanged but warm the climate by altitude
raise atmospheric oxygen and stop all volcanic outgassing
questions.explanation: Weathering of silicate rocks draws carbon dioxide from the air, and the carbon ends up in ocean carbonates. Faster weathering over geological time therefore cools the climate, showing how tectonics affects climate.

questions.stem: Which driver is matched with the timescale over which it changes climate?
options: Orbital cycles: a few years to a decade
El Niño and La Niña: tens of thousands of years each cycle
Ocean gateway changes: a few months
Plate tectonic supercycle: hundreds of millions of years
questions.explanation: Climate changes are evident at a variety of timescales: ENSO acts over years, orbital cycles over tens of thousands of years, and tectonic changes over millions to hundreds of millions of years.

questions.stem: Which two human activities are the main causes of increased greenhouse gases in the atmosphere?
options: Building dams and desalinating water
Mining iron ore and smelting nickel only
Irrigating crops and planting forests
Burning fossil fuels and clearing land
questions.explanation: Burning coal, oil and gas releases carbon that was stored for millions of years, and land clearing releases carbon stored in vegetation and soil while removing a carbon sink.

questions.stem: Which human activity is a major source of methane?
options: Using refrigerators, which leak methane from their cooling systems
Planting forests, which release methane from their leaves at night
Digestion by cattle and sheep, which release methane as they belch
Burning petrol in cars, which releases methane as the main exhaust gas
questions.explanation: Methane comes from livestock digestion, rice paddies, landfill and leaks from gas and coal operations. Car exhaust is mainly carbon dioxide and water vapour.

questions.stem: Nitrous oxide concentrations in the atmosphere have risen mainly because of:
options: the cooling of lava flows from volcanoes
the use of nitrogen fertilisers in agriculture
the melting of glaciers in mountain ranges
the release of salt spray from ocean waves
questions.explanation: Soil microbes convert part of the nitrogen in fertiliser into nitrous oxide, a long-lived and potent greenhouse gas.

questions.stem: Hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs) were introduced to replace CFCs in refrigeration and air conditioning. Why are they still a concern?
options: They do not destroy ozone, but they are very potent greenhouse gases
They destroy far more ozone than CFCs, but they do not trap any heat
They are produced naturally by forests, so their levels cannot be controlled
They break down in a few minutes, so they react to form carbon monoxide
questions.explanation: HFCs contain no chlorine, so they do not deplete stratospheric ozone, but each molecule traps far more heat than a molecule of carbon dioxide. Their use is now being phased down.

questions.stem: How does clearing native forest for farmland increase atmospheric carbon dioxide?
options: Crops release far more carbon dioxide than forests during photosynthesis
Clearing exposes rock that releases carbon dioxide by chemical weathering
Burning or decay releases stored carbon, and fewer trees remain to absorb it
Cleared soil absorbs carbon dioxide, so the plants above release even more
questions.explanation: Trees and soils are carbon stores. Clearing turns them into a source as wood burns or decays, and replaces a long-lived carbon sink with short-lived crops.

questions.stem: Which statement describes the enhanced greenhouse effect linked to human activities?
options: The cooling of Earth by aerosols that reflect sunlight back to space after eruptions
Damage to the ozone layer that lets more ultraviolet radiation reach Earth's surface
Extra warming as rising greenhouse gas levels absorb more outgoing infrared and re-emit it
The natural warming of Earth's surface by water vapour, without which the whole Earth would freeze
questions.explanation: The natural greenhouse effect keeps Earth habitable. Human emissions increase greenhouse gas concentrations, so more infrared radiation is redirected towards the surface and temperatures rise further.

questions.stem: Carbon dioxide measured at a remote observatory shows a steady rise every year, with a small up-and-down cycle within each year. What causes the yearly cycle?
options: The oceans boil off carbon dioxide each summer and absorb it all back each winter
Volcanoes erupt every northern summer, adding carbon dioxide on a regular cycle
Northern Hemisphere plants absorb carbon dioxide in their growing season and release it later
Fossil fuel use stops completely each northern winter, then restarts each year in spring and summer
questions.explanation: Most land vegetation is in the Northern Hemisphere. Photosynthesis in its spring and summer draws carbon dioxide down, and decay in autumn and winter releases it, superimposed on the long-term rise.

questions.stem: Ice cores show atmospheric carbon dioxide stayed between about 180 and 300 ppm for the last 800 000 years. Today it is well above 400 ppm. What does this indicate?
options: Carbon dioxide has been falling, so the climate should be cooling now
Current levels lie well outside the natural range of the last 800 000 years
Current levels are normal, because they lie within the natural glacial range
Ice cores must be unreliable, because levels above 300 ppm cannot occur
questions.explanation: Air trapped in ice records past atmospheric composition. Present concentrations are far higher than at any time in this long record, and the rise matches the timing of industrial emissions.

questions.stem: The ratio of carbon-13 to carbon-12 in atmospheric carbon dioxide has been falling as carbon dioxide rises. Fossil fuels are depleted in carbon-13. What does this suggest?
options: The added carbon dioxide comes mainly from volcanic eruptions
The added carbon dioxide is coming out of the warming oceans
The carbon dioxide is being converted into carbon-13 in the air
The added carbon dioxide comes largely from burning fossil fuels
questions.explanation: Fossil fuels formed from plants, which take up less carbon-13, so their carbon is isotopically light. Adding it lowers the atmosphere's carbon-13 ratio, an isotopic fingerprint of the source. The oceans are absorbing carbon dioxide overall, not releasing it.

questions.stem: Soot from fires and diesel engines settles on snow and glaciers. How does this affect climate?
options: It has no effect, because particulates fall out of the atmosphere before reaching snow
It darkens the surface, lowering albedo, so more sunlight is absorbed and melting speeds up
It brightens the surface, raising albedo, so more sunlight is reflected and ice grows faster
It insulates the ice, so the snow beneath stays frozen however warm the air becomes
questions.explanation: Particulate materials can change climate. Dark particles on ice absorb sunlight, warming and melting the surface, while reflective aerosols such as sulfates in the air have a cooling effect.

questions.stem: Which two processes are the main causes of global sea level rise as the climate warms?
options: Increased rainfall over oceans and thicker sea ice
Rising sea floor at ridges and faster tidal currents
Thermal expansion of seawater and melting of ice on land
Melting of floating sea ice and increased river runoff
questions.explanation: Water expands as it warms, and melting glaciers and ice sheets add water that was stored on land. Floating sea ice already displaces its own weight of water.

questions.stem: Why does melting of floating Arctic sea ice add almost nothing to sea level, while melting of the Greenland ice sheet raises it?
options: Arctic sea ice is made of salt, which sinks to the sea floor when the ice melts
Greenland's ice is denser than seawater, so it takes up much more space when it melts
Arctic sea ice evaporates directly into the air instead of melting into the sea
Floating ice already displaces its weight of water, but Greenland's ice sits on land
questions.explanation: Ice floating in the sea has already pushed aside its own mass of water, so melting it barely changes sea level. Ice on land adds new water to the ocean when it melts or flows into the sea.

questions.stem: As the climate warms, many species are recorded further south along Western Australia's coast than before. Which explanation fits?
options: Species are being moved by ships, so climate change cannot explain any range shifts
Species are evolving new body plans within a single generation to suit the warmth
Species are shifting their ranges towards the poles to stay within suitable temperatures
Species are shifting towards the equator because the southern coastal waters have become cooler
questions.explanation: Climate change has been linked to changes in species distribution. On land and in the sea, many organisms are moving poleward or to higher altitudes as their preferred conditions shift.

questions.stem: Winter rainfall in south-west Western Australia has declined since the 1970s. Which change is linked to this decline?
options: A southward shift of the winter rain-bearing fronts and higher pressure over the region
A northward shift of the monsoon, bringing more tropical storms south to Perth in each winter
A rise in the number of tropical cyclones crossing the south coast each winter
A cooling of the Indian Ocean that has stopped all evaporation off the west coast
questions.explanation: More frequent high pressure and a southward shift of the westerly storm track mean fewer cold fronts reach the south-west in winter. This shows climate change altering rainfall patterns regionally.

questions.stem: Higher carbon dioxide can increase the growth of some crops, yet projections for Western Australian wheat yields are not simply positive. Why?
options: Wheat cannot use carbon dioxide at all, so higher levels always reduce its growth directly in every season
Higher carbon dioxide makes rainfall more reliable, so crops grow too fast and fall over
Carbon dioxide is toxic to all crops at any concentration above pre-industrial levels
Hotter, drier conditions and more heat stress during flowering can outweigh any carbon dioxide benefit
questions.explanation: Climate change has been linked to changes in crop productivity. Reduced rainfall and hot spells at critical growth stages can lower yields even if extra carbon dioxide boosts photosynthesis.

questions.stem: As global temperatures rise, Arctic sea ice shrinks and exposes dark ocean water. Why does this speed up warming?
options: Dark water has a higher albedo than ice, so it reflects more infrared back to the surface
Ice releases carbon dioxide when it melts, which is the only cause of the extra warming
Open water stops evaporation, so latent heat is no longer carried away from the surface
Dark water has a lower albedo than ice, so it absorbs more sunlight and warms further
questions.explanation: This is the ice-albedo feedback, a positive feedback. Changes in global ice cover therefore amplify warming or cooling, which climate models must include.

questions.stem: Temperatures in the Arctic have risen considerably faster than the global average. What does this show?
options: The Arctic is the only region where climate change has occurred
Temperature records from the Arctic must be completely unreliable
Climate change affects different regions to different degrees
Global average temperature has not changed at all over time
questions.explanation: Feedbacks such as loss of snow and ice make warming stronger at high northern latitudes. Records show climate change has affected regions and species differently.

questions.stem: What do air bubbles trapped in ice cores record?
options: The number of volcanic eruptions on other continents during the past century
The speed of the wind at the time each snow layer fell on the ice sheet
The composition of the atmosphere, such as carbon dioxide and methane, when the ice formed
The temperature of the ocean surface directly below the ice sheet at the time the snow fell
questions.explanation: As snow compacts into ice, it seals in small samples of air. Analysing them gives past greenhouse gas concentrations over hundreds of thousands of years.

questions.stem: In an ice core, layers with a lower ratio of oxygen-18 to oxygen-16 than average indicate:
options: heavier volcanic activity during that period
colder air temperatures when that snow fell
warmer air temperatures when that snow fell
higher carbon dioxide levels in that period
questions.explanation: Water containing heavy oxygen-18 condenses and falls out more readily as air cools on its way to the poles, so snow falling in colder times is depleted in oxygen-18.

questions.stem: During glacial periods, the shells of foraminifera in ocean sediments have a higher ratio of oxygen-18 to oxygen-16, the opposite of ice cores. Why?
options: Ice sheets store water rich in oxygen-16, leaving the oceans relatively enriched in oxygen-18
Foraminifera grow only in warm water, so all glacial-age shells must come from tropical seas
Oxygen-18 is produced in seawater by cosmic rays, which become much stronger during glacials
Ice sheets release oxygen-18 into the oceans as they grow during glacial periods
questions.explanation: Water evaporated from the sea is enriched in light oxygen-16, and during glacials much of it is locked in ice sheets. The remaining seawater, and the shells built from it, become richer in oxygen-18.

questions.stem: Why are pollen grains preserved in lake sediments useful evidence of past climate?
options: They record the exact air temperature on the day each grain fell into the lake water
They are produced only during ice ages, so their presence shows glacial conditions
They contain trapped air that records past carbon dioxide levels in the atmosphere above the lake
They are tough and distinctive, so they show which plants, and so which climate, existed
questions.explanation: Pollen walls resist decay and can usually be identified to plant group. Changes in the mix of pollen through a sediment core reveal changes in vegetation, which reflect climate.

questions.stem: Rocks about 50 million years old in Antarctica, which was then already near the South Pole, contain fossil leaves of broadleaf forest trees. What does this indicate?
options: Fossil leaves can travel thousands of kilometres in the wind
The polar climate was then much warmer than it is today
Antarctica was then located at the equator, not the pole
The trees grew under ice, so the climate was the same as now
questions.explanation: Forests cannot grow on an ice sheet, so fossils of forest trees at polar latitudes indicate a much warmer climate. Fossils are one of the geological records of past climate change.

questions.stem: A researcher wants to reconstruct year-by-year rainfall over the past 400 years at one site. Which record would be most suitable?
options: Air bubbles from ice cores that span the last 800 000 years
Tree rings from long-lived trees, checked against historical records
Fossil leaves from rocks hundreds of millions of years old
Oxygen isotopes in deep-sea sediments covering a million years
questions.explanation: Ring width reflects each year's growing conditions, giving annual resolution over centuries. Historical records help calibrate them. The other records cover much longer periods at much coarser resolution.

questions.stem: Pollen records from two lakes on opposite sides of a continent cover the same 10 000 years. One shows forest replaced by grassland; the other shows almost no change. Which conclusion is best?
options: No climate change occurred, because the two records do not show the same trend at both lakes
The forest at one site was replaced by grassland only because pollen decays faster in grassland
Climate change affected the two regions differently, so one site cannot represent the whole continent
One record must be wrong, because climate change affects every region in exactly the same way
questions.explanation: Geological and prehistorical records show that climate change has affected regions and species differently over time. Conclusions need records from many sites.

questions.stem: How does a general circulation model (GCM) simulate the climate?
options: It averages past weather observations and assumes the future will repeat them exactly as before
It counts tree rings from around the world and extends the trend into the future
It uses a single equation for global temperature that ignores oceans and ice
It divides the atmosphere and oceans into a 3D grid and solves physical equations for each cell
questions.explanation: GCMs apply the laws of physics to the movement of energy, water and air between grid cells over time. They are developed using past and current climate data.

questions.stem: Before a climate model is used to project future climate, it is run from 1900 to the present and its output compared with observed temperatures. Why?
options: To change the observed temperatures so that they match the model exactly for that period
To calculate future emissions directly from the temperatures observed since 1900
To prove that the model's projections will be exactly correct for every future year
To test whether the model reproduces past climate, which builds confidence in its projections
questions.explanation: This is called hindcasting. A model that reproduces observed changes when given known natural and human influences is more trustworthy, though projections still carry uncertainty.

questions.stem: Which is a major source of uncertainty in projections of future global temperature?
options: Whether the laws of physics will still apply in coming decades
Whether carbon dioxide absorbs infrared radiation at all
Whether Earth will continue to orbit the Sun for a century
Future greenhouse gas emissions and how clouds respond to warming
questions.explanation: Projections depend on how much people emit and on feedbacks that are hard to model, especially clouds. The basic physics of greenhouse gases is well established.

questions.stem: Australian forecasters run models of El Niño and La Niña using ocean temperature and wind data. Why are these models useful?
options: They prevent El Niño from developing by identifying where to cool the Pacific Ocean
They replace long-term climate models, since ENSO controls all climate change
They forecast ENSO conditions months ahead, informing seasonal rainfall and temperature outlooks
They predict exactly how much rain each farm will receive on each and every day of the coming year
questions.explanation: Models of ocean-atmosphere interaction can forecast the development of El Niño or La Niña, which strongly affects Australian rainfall, helping farmers and water managers plan.

questions.stem: Observations showed some ice sheets losing mass faster than older models had projected. Scientists then improved how the models represent ice flow. What does this show about climate models?
options: They are designed to overestimate change, so observations always fall below projections
They are revised as new evidence and better understanding of their assumptions become available
They are unreliable and should be abandoned, since any mismatch proves the science is wrong
They are fixed once published, so new observations cannot change their projections
questions.explanation: Models of long-term climate trends are subject to debate and revision based on supporting evidence and review of their underlying assumptions and limitations. Improving them is normal science.
